optionReasons.saa-ini-080:option:0: 'Compressing the source servers' is not a real mechanism — compression is CONTENT, not server.
optionReasons.saa-ini-080:option:2: The CloudFront does not create instances EC2 — He's a cache layer, not an orchestrator..
optionReasons.saa-ini-080:option:3: The CloudFront does not block viewers by origin limit — it absorbs demand in cache.

finalJustifications: Because the edge locations respond to the local cache (hit) and only the miss caches arrive at the origin — the load at the origin collapses even with thousands of viewers.
Because CloudFront replicates the source servers on each continent, distributing the live transmission processing.
Because CloudFront threads the surplus spectators in a waiting room, releasing the origin to serve in lots.
Because CloudFront copy the transmission to S3 automatically and starts serving the direct video segments of the pocket.

optionReasons.saa-ini-105:option:0: Geolocation divides by country/region of user — not by percentage ratio.
optionReasons.saa-ini-105:option:1: Failover is all-or-nothing with health check — doesn't divide 90/10.
optionReasons.saa-ini-105:option:2: Latency-based chooses the fastest region for each user — the proportion is not controllable.

finalJustifications: Because weighted routing attributes weights to records (90/10) and allows you to adjust them gradually — the classic mechanism of canary release via DNS.
Because weighted routing measures the error rate of the new version and adjusts the weights alone, accelerating or reversing the rollout.
Because weighted routing directs beta users registered to the new version, keeping the general public in the current one.
Because weighted routing balances by the computational capacity of each set, sending 10% because they are smaller servers.

optionReasons.saa-ini-122:option:0: The CloudFront Accelerates HAZARDABLE CONTENT — Doesn't give static IPs anycast to fail instant endpoints.
optionReasons.saa-ini-122:option:2: Direct Connect connect the client's datacenter to AWS — nothing to do with global user routing.
optionReasons.saa-ini-122:option:3: Latency-based routing is DNS: dependent on TTL to propagate changes — precisely the limitation that you want to avoid.

finalJustifications: Because Global Accelerator uses anycast STATUS IPs and redirects almost instantly to the nearest healthy endpoint — without expecting propagation of DNS.
Because Global Accelerator update records DNS with TTL of 1 second, propagating the fallover almost instantly.
Because Global Accelerator caches the responses of the ALBs on the edges, serving users without consulting the regions.
Because Global Accelerator migrating ALB whole to the nearest region of the user, eliminating the route distance.

optionReasons.saa-ini-141:option:0: TTL short to TUDO throws out the benefit of the cache of images — the origin goes to be consulted for nothing.
optionReasons.saa-ini-141:option:1: Disabling the cache resolves the stock but sacrifices everything — the problem is granularity, not cache itself.
optionReasons.saa-ini-141:option:3: A second distribution works, but it's unnecessary complexity — cache behaviors solve in MESMA distribution.

finalJustifications: Because cache behaviors by path pattern allow TTL long for /images/* and TTL short (or no cache) for the JSON of stock — in the same distribution.
Because cache behaviors automatically detect which files have changed at source and only renew affected entries.
Because the cache behaviors compress the JSON of stock, and compressed articles expire more rapidly in edge locations.
Because behavior caches invalidate the entire distribution to each stock update, forcing the refresh of images.

optionReasons.saa-ini-145:option:1: It's the closest because it's also a configuration adjustment of itself. CloudFront — but TTL 0 only constant revalidation force at source: increases traffic and does not reduce the TAMANHO of files; who reduces the transferred bytes is automatic compression (gzip/Brotli).
optionReasons.saa-ini-145:option:2: HTTPS encrypts transport — doesn't compress anything.
optionReasons.saa-ini-145:option:3: Field-Level Encryption protects sensitive fields from forms — does not reduce JS size/CSS.

finalJustifications: Because the automatic compression of the CloudFront delivery JS/CSS/HTML in Gzip/Brotli when the browser supports — less bytes in the network without pre-compressing at source.
Because the compression of the CloudFront reduces the resolution of images automatically, adapting the weight of the page to each connection.
Because automatic compression depends on Origin Shield enabled, the layer where the objects are compressed before the edges.
Because CloudFront minify JavaScript code on borders, removing comments and spaces before delivering to browsers.

optionReasons.saa-ini-154:option:0: Lambda@Edge executes code on the edge — not a layer of CACHE consolidated; responding without origin would require reimplementing the content.
optionReasons.saa-ini-154:option:2: Field-Level Encryption protects sensitive data — nothing to do with load at source.
optionReasons.saa-ini-154:option:3: No longer enabled edge locations' manually — and more edges would even increase the simultaneous miss caches.

finalJustifications: Because the Origin Shield is an extra central layer of cache: the misses of various edges converge on it, and the origin receives a fraction of the requests.
Because the Origin Shield replicates the origin in three regions automatically, dividing the miss caches between the new copies.
Because the Origin Shield thread the simultaneous requests and deliver them to the origin one by one, at the pace it supports.
Because the Origin Shield locks the miss caches to the TTL of the expiring object, serving the previous version while this.

optionReasons.saa-ini-215:option:0: The CloudFront USA certificates, but who issues/renews is the ACM — the distribution does not provide alone.
optionReasons.saa-ini-215:option:2: The Route 53 management DNS and domain records — does not issue certificates.
optionReasons.saa-ini-215:option:3: The IAM accepts to import certificates (legacy), but DO NOT automatically renew.

finalJustifications: Because ACM issue free certificates for ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway and, with validation DNS, renew everything automatically — zero manual management.
Because ACM installs certificates within the instances EC2, renewing the application keystore at each expiration.
Because ACM issues valid certificates by 10 years, which in practice dispenses with any process of renewal.
Because ACM is mandatory for domains registered in AWS, and the renewal is embedded in the annual rate of Route 53.

optionReasons.saa-ini-239:option:0: It seems plausible because Weighted Routing is another real policy of Route 53 capable of sending 100% from traffic to backup — but would require someone MUDAR the weights manually after failure; only Failover Routing with health checks redirects itself when the primary falls.
optionReasons.saa-ini-239:option:1: Geolocation route by user location — not health backup mechanism.
optionReasons.saa-ini-239:option:2: Latency routing chooses the lowest latency between regions — does not monitor primary server failure.

finalJustifications: Because Failover Routing uses health check at Primary and, when detecting failure, starts responding with Secondary in DNS Responses — automatic failover.
Because Failover Routing restarts the primary server via automation before alternating, solving the source failure.
Because Failover Routing divides traffic 50/50 between the two servers until the primary responds healthy again.
Because Failover Routing synchronizes primary data to backup, ensuring consistency before diversion.
